subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR THE SUPPRESSION OF ILLICIT TRAFFIC IN DANGEROUS DRUGS, SIGNED AT GENEVA, JUNE 26, 1936

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: APPROVAL OF CONVENTION FOR THE SUPPRESSION OF ILLICIT TRAFFIC IN DANGEROUS DRUGS, SIGNED AT GENEVA, JUNE 26, 1936
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the convention of 1936 for the suppression of the illicit traffic in dangerous drugs (Geneva, June 26, 1936), signed on behalf of Canada by the plenipotentiary named therein, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I mentioned yesterday, the subject-matter of t' e convention was considered by the house at the time the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Power) introduced his bill with respect to opium and narcotic drugs. That was in February of this year. The bill was to implement any obligation on the part of Canada which might be incurred under the terms of the convention. Its main purpose is to make more severe the penalties which have existed in the past with respect to illicit trafficking in opium and other drugs.
The convention was drawn up by the international conference for the suppression of the illicit traffic in dangerous drugs which met in Geneva under the auspices of the League of Nations. The objectives of the conference were, first, to secure international cooperation in stiffening penalties for breaches of legislation implementing the earlier opium con-

Bank of Canada
ventions of 1912, 1925 and 1931, and, secondly, to strengthen police efforts to repress the illicit traffic in narcotic drugs.
The draft before the conference was the result of two years' preparatory work initiated by the opium advisory committee. A first draft had been submitted to all governments signatory to the opium conventions in 1934. Their observations and criticisms were taken into consideration in preparing a revised draft which was circulated in 1935. It was only after this thorough canvass of the competent national authorities had established the expediency of endeavouring to draw up an international convention that the decision to hold the special conference was taken.
The Canadian government was represented at this conference by Colonel C. H. L. Shar-man, chief of the narcotics division, Department of Pensions and National Health, who is also the Canadian representative on the opium advisory committee and who had taken an active part in the preparatory discussions of the draft convention.
The convention requires ratification. It will enter into force ninety days after the secretary general of the league has received the ratifications or accessions of ten states.
It has been signed on behalf of thirty-two countries and ratification has been completed, up to date, by India, China and Belgium.
When parliament has approved the convention the governor in council will authorize ratification.
I do not know that I need say much more. If hon. members wish to know the main provisions of the convention I can give them by quoting one or -two of its articles. The convention itself has been distributed among hon. members, and that may not, therefore, be necessary.
Motion agreed to.

subtopic: CONFIRMATION OF CERTAIN AGREEMENTS BETWEEN DOMINION GOVERNMENT AND PROVINCES OF MANITOBA, SASKATCHEWAN AND ALBERTA- CONCURRENCE IN SENATE AMENDMENTS
speechtext:
The amendments made in
the Senate are really for the purpose of meeting what I conceive to be a valid objection as to the exercise of its powers by this parliament. Whether or not that is being done I am in doubt. The proposed amendments provide that this act shall be read and construed as one with the following acts: The Manitoba Natural Resources Act, the Alberta Natural Resources Acts, and the Saskatchewan Natural Resources Acts. The effect of that is to seek to remedy the difficulty to which attention was directed and treat the amendments now made as though it were part of the original agreement, so that they should be read together as one agreement. Whether or not that is achieved I have some doubt, but certainly it does give a semblance of authority to this parliament to deal with it by endeavouring to make it appear that the proposals now made were proposals that appeared in the original agreements. To that extent I am certain that it does greatly improve the situation; but I still have grave doubts as to whether it may not be considered an amendment of the constitution. That in itself requires the approval of the imperial parliament to give it validity, in view of the fact that we did specially reserve the water under the lands, and did not include it in the transfer of resources. Kingston has been a stormy spot in the politics of this country ever since I can remember coming to this chamber, so far as patronage is concerned. I can recall in 1911 and 1912 the difficulties in connection with the penitentiary, and I recall too the charges made by the late member for Kingston, Doctor Ross, as to the lack of attention to patronage matters by the late administration.
Great hopes and expectations were raised when it became apparent that one who had the high qualifications of the present Minister of Labour was to stand as candidate in Kingston. I therefore made myself the promise that I would watch and see whether or not these high hopes and expectations would be realized or whether what is known as the machine would crush the minister, and he would be overborne by it, rather than overbear it; whether or not the political patronage committee in Kingston would be able to compel the minister to conform to their mind, or whether he would be able to give effect to those high principles, those noble sentiments he expressed so frequently during the campaign.

August 23, 1935. The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett,

Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
My dear Chief:
I have just come in from the constituencies of Lisgar, Provencher and St. Boniface particularly, and the situation at the moment is very good there politically, but it needs the necessary impetus to carry on.
I have already written to the Hon. J. E. Lawson, the Hon. R. J. Manion and the Hon. Wesley Gordon and the Hon. T. G. Murphy with regard to the two roads in these three constituencies that are vital factors in this election campaign, and they have the whole story in detail, both verbally and in writing.
In 1931 the federal government appropriated moneys for both of these roads. Both trunk highways enter the province of Manitoba, and as an unemployment relief measure, quite considerable work was done, which 1 think was shared by the federal and provincial governments fifty per cent each. The provincial government have or did apply again for these two roads to be carried on as an unemployment relief measure, but for some reason or other were more or less turned down as a matter of policy.
A new problem has arisen lately, which may be a good reason for reconsideration. As you know rust and extreme heat have destroyed the larger portion of our Manitoba wheat crop, and in some parts of Lisgar and Provencher especially it has created a very serious problem, and has left the farmers in a serious situation. My thought is that if your government will cooperate with the provincial government as an unemployment relief works measure, that work could be done on these roads that would give the farmers of these three constituencies plenty to do and help them to earn something, whereas if it is not done they possibly may appeal to the provincial and federal governments for some form of relief and for which we will get nothing, but on the other hand are perfectly willing to work themselves and use their teams and equipment. As a political measure, it assures us without any question of a doubt these three seats which we badly want to win, and which look very good for us at the present time.
The Liberal federal members in these three constituencies, supported to some extent, under cover, by provincial government members, are endeavouring to blame the federal government for the fact that these two roads have not and will not be built, and it has become such a strong factor politically, that a great deal rests on a favourable decision being made.
I feel that we should play the game politically, call the provincial government's bluff, who have stated positively to delegates that they are prepared to put up dollar for dollar with the federal government in the building of these two roads as an unemployment relief works measure, and I understand, although I am not sure, that the provincial government have forwarded on letters of approval for both of these

During the election campaign of 1935 we were faced with the project of a road running through my constituency from Russell to Erickson, joining with the Clear Lake road to Riding Mountain. Let me give my right hon. friend an illustration.
I know what I am talking about.

When this park was opened, invitations were sent all around, but they were so anxious to keep out Liberals that they did not even invite the three members who had secured the park for Manitoba, the hon. member for Dauphin, the hon. member for Neepawa and myself.

You were not members of the house at that time.

We were not members of the house, but we had secured the park for Manitoba. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did not hear that; he experienced that.
It is hearsay.

That is what was happening
all the time. Let me give another illustration. This story was told to me as being true. The Hon. Mr. Murphy certainly did well for the constituency of Neepawa. He provided plenty of jobs in that park. The day after the election when he was defeated, a man came up to the garage man in Neepawa and said to him, "What happened yesterday at the election? I am afraid that is a
manufactured story. That story originated in the United States.

It was told to me as the
truth.

That story is told in
every election.

I want to refer to the principle that was involved in the construction of works under the leader of the opposition. I do not know that there has ever been a time when one could say more positively: Here is political patronage at its very worst. A letter was sent from Mr. Webb, a gentleman who had been mayor I believe seven times and who is now a member of the provincial legislature, to the head of the federal government of that day, stating reasons why certain roads should be built. That request was granted by the leader of the government of that day. It has been suggested to me that they were to be started before October 10. I think it ill behooves the right hon. leader of the opposition to take the position he has taken to-day with regard to matters in the constituency of the Minister of Labour.

If he had shown the same desire and regard in the past for proper dealing, then his argument to-day might have been much stronger. I do not defend patronage of that kind and I do not practise it. My constituents tell me that there are Tories now working in this park when a Liberal could not get a job during the Tory administration. I am being blamed for that. I agree with the statement made by the Prime Minister to the effect that we should endeavour to eliminate patronage in all forms of the civil and political service. I agree that we ought to do that in our political and public life. I believe the leader of the opposition has been ill advised in bringing to light these matters at a time when he is passing from public life. I felt I had to say what I have said because I know the facts in connection with patronage in that park.

When this item was under consideration last year the minister intimated that he had under advisement an extension of the follow-up service with regard to the placement of young women, particularly in domestic service. I should like to know what steps have been taken to implement the assurance given last year?

I do not recall the precise
statement to which my hon. friend refers. The federal government does not appoint the personnel in the various provincial employment offices. This is simply going over the ground that we covered yesterday when this item was under discussion. I shall be glad to look up the point mentioned by my hon. friend. There has been certainly no intentional oversight with respect to the matter, but I do not recall at the moment the precise point raised last year.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Before this item carries, may I ask the right hon. leader of the opposition if, in view of the existence of the documents that have been read and placed on Hansard, and the statements contained therein which reveal a conspiracy to use public funds to corrupt the electorate in three constituencies on the part of himself and three other ministers of the crown when he was occupying the office of Prime Minister, he has nothing to say in defence of his action before this matter is allowed to drop?

The observations that
I shall make will be made when the house resumes this evening. There is no warrant for any such language as that used by the Prime Minister. What is more, there is no authority for his statement in the letters that

Private Bills

A copy of that letter was read in this house by the right hon. gentleman's mouthpiece. The right hon. gentleman would not do it. He would not disgrace himself by doing that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: When the house rose at six o'clock the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), speaking in reference to the correspondence which had been read to the committee by the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien), made the statement that I myself would not have read this correspondence to the committee, but that I was using the hon. member for Provencher as-henchman I think was the expression used.
No, "mouthpiece" was the word I used.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As a mouthpiece to perform that service on my behalf. I wish to say at once that I had no word direct or indirect with the hon. member for Provencher with reference to his action in the committee to-day. I never said a word to him about any of the correspondence; I did not instruct anyone else to say a word to him on my behalf. His action was entirely his own as far as I know. That is the truth with regard to that matter.
Now, with respect to what actually took place, as will be recalled, some time ago an order was passed by this house for a return showing certain correspondence. This is what was called for and what was brought
3738	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
down. It was brought down, yesterday, a return to an address to the House of Commons dated June 6, 1938 showing:
-a copy of all letters, telegrams, orders, in council, agreements and other documents having to do with the construction of the Piney highway, Morden Sprague highway, Brandon Clear Lake highway, in Manitoba, carried on between the province of Manitoba and the dominion government, as well as all other correspondence in relation thereto, between the Minister of Labour, the Prime Minister and any other parties, between the dates of August 20, 1935, and October 15, 1935.
That was the correspondence which this house ordered should be tabled, correspondence to be taken from the files of the government department. The Minister of Labour, performing his obligation as a minister of the crown to bring down the correspondence asked for by this house, undoubtedly requested his deputy minister or some other official in his department to bring to him or to send to the Secretary of State all the correspondence on file and to have that correspondence prepared so that it might be tabled in this house by the Secretary of State, who would subsequently table it. The correspondence that was tabled came from the office of the Minister of Labour. It was all correspondence that related to the subject which this house had ordered should be dealt with in the return. The correspondence dated back to previous years and was laid on the table exactly as taken from the files of the department, not those of the present minister but in part those of the previous minister, the files that he had left in the department as a matter of record to justify his actions. I ask the committee to keep that circumstance in mind. We are being told by the right hon. leader of the opposition that certain letters which were on the files of the ex-Minister of Labour, and which he had left in the department as a record to justify his course, should not have been brought down.
I did not say and did not suggest that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is the insinuation.
I did not suggest it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Then we will come to what was actually done. What was the correspondence that was there? Here was the first communication, and I will ask the right hon. leader of the opposition if he will say that this letter should not have been brought down:

Conservative Dominion Headquarters Province of Manitoba
408 McIntyre Block, Winnipeg, Man., August 23, 1935.
The Hon. Wesley Gordon, ICC., M.P.,
Minister of Labour,
Ottawa, Ontario.
Dear Mr. Gordon:
I would appreciate it very much indeed if you would kindly read the enclosed carefully. It does explain the situation and means so much to us, and in view of the new conditions that have arisen owing to the rust and extreme heat on the crops, it might be good justification for really doing something at this time as a special consideration. There is not the question of a doubt that if we do not do something many hundreds and thousands of these people in these districts will be applying to the provincial and federal governments for assistance this winter.
Yours very truly,
R. H. Webb,
Director for Manitoba.
I ask the right hon. leader of the opposition: Does he say the Minister of Labour should not have brought down that letter, when it was in the files; a letter making a straight appeal from one who, if I am not mistaken, was at the time the mayor of Winnipeg, or who certainly had held that position for many years; a letter addressed to the minister in his capacity as a minister of the crown; making an appeal to the Minister of Labour to do a certain thing to help relieve a situation; to use money of the federal government, which was intended for relief purposes, in order to provide for the construction of roads.
That is not marked "confidential" either.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am just
coming to that. This letter is not marked "personal and confidential." It was on the file as a public letter, a strictly official letter. It is not for me to say anything about what were the relations between the former Prime Minister and his colleagues, but I have pretty good reason for saying that Hon. Mr. Gordon, I have no doubt, felt the necessity of protecting himself with regard to all actions that were taken by his department; and I assume one reason why he left this letter on the file-if there was any reason why it should not be left there-was that he felt the necessity of being able to affirm what it was which occasioned the action that was taken. Now may I come to the next letter, but first let me refer again to these lines:
I would appreciate it very much indeed if you would kindly read the enclosed carefully. It does explain the situation and means so much to us . . .

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
"Read the enclosed carefully." What is the enclosed? There is only one enclosure, and that is the document which the leader of the opposition says should not have been brought down. He says that I would not have produced it, but that I had my mouthpiece, as he said, read it instead. I ask hon. members of the committee how the Minister of Labour, being ordered by the house to produce the documents that were on the file of the ex-Minister of Labour and lay them on the table, could have taken out of that file a communication that was not marked personal or private or a communication which was attached to a letter, which was referred to therein as "the enclosed" and which, it was stated, was placed there in order to explain the situation and explain it very carefully. The enclosure, when one looks at it, is not so much a personal, private letter. A personal, private letter is a communication that is sent to one person for his personal, private information, not to be passed on to others. This letter was much more in the nature of a circular than a personal, private letter. It was a circular letter to other ministers of the government of the day. It is headed:
Copy to the Hon. Wesley Gordon, K.C., M.P., Ottawa, Ontario.
Copy to the Hon. J. Earl Lawson, K.C., M.P., Ottawa, Ontario.
Copy to the Hon. Dr. R. J. Manion, M.P., Ottawa, Ontario.
Then after the words, "private and personal," and the date, August 23, 1935, there is the address:
The Right Hon. R. B. Bennett, P.C., K.C., M.P.,
Prime Minister of Canada,
Ottawa, Ontario.
It is written to the right hon. gentleman as Prime Minister, and begins:
My dear Chief:
I need not read the whole of the letter, but here are some of the essential parts; this is what Mr. Webb was telling the Minister of Labour he must consider as the reasons why the government of the day should appropriate a large sum of money for the construction of certain roads. The amount, I believe, was something like SI,365,000, and here are the reasons set forth why that amount should be appropriated for the purpose mentioned: My dear Chief:
I have just come in from the constituencies of Lisgar, Provencher and St. Boniface particularly, and the situation at the moment is very good there politically, but it needs the necessary impetus to carry on.
I have already written to the Hon. J. Earl Lawson, the Hon. Dr. R. J. Manion and the Hon. Wesley Gordon and the Hon. T. G.
Murphy with regard to the two roads in these three constituencies that are vital factors in this election campaign, and they have the whole story in detail, both verbally and in writing.
The house is denied the whole story as the ministers of the crown of that day had it. I am not at all sure that it would not be advisable for us to call the public accounts committee together and get the whole story.
I agree with the right hon. leader of the opposition that this business of trying to corrupt and bribe constituencies with public money is something that must be stopped if it possibly can be; but I do not think to that end we need waste the time of this House of Commons as it has been wasted in these last two days with the right hon. leader of the opposition devoting two complete sessions of this house to what? To talking about what I think is generally described as one of the lowest forms of ward politics; insinuations as to how this man and that man, whose names are unknown to anyone or were unknown until placed on Hansard to-day, received or were denied this or that consideration, or were expected to do this or that for some political reason. I say it is wasting the time of this parliament to talk of that sort of thing when you have the written evidence that a prime minister and several of his colleagues sat together and conspired-* that is not too strong a word-to see how three constituencies in a province could be won, by means of money appropriated by this parliament for purposes of relief, and worked hand in glove to that end with the political organizer of a province. That is the kind of thing that needs looking into, and that is the sort of thing that needs to be stopped. That is what we have in the correspondence tabled to-day. Let me read more: As a political measure, it assures us without any question of a doubt these three seats which we badly want to win, and which look very good for us at the present time. ... I feel that we should play the game politically . . . If the federal government would advise of participation in these two roads, it would be good politics; it would call the provincial government's bluff; it would kill the propaganda that the Liberals are carrying on at the present time; it would assure us of a victory in these three seats and-
Then comes-and I do not think it is too strong a term to use-the most contemptible part of it all:
-and in my humble opinion will not have cost the federal government anything, because by the time the work is organized the election will be over, and winter will be upon us, and perhaps very little work will have been done before the end of the present fiscal year.
Ending up with:
And politically it means victory for us.

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
The right hon. the leader of the opposition said he was watching with interest to see whether the new Minister of Labour, with his high ideals in public life, would be able to destroy the machine, the political machine, or whether he would be overborne or crushed by it. And yet the leader of the opposition himself when Prime Minister of this country was conspiring with his colleagues not only to help that political machine, but to oil it and to give it power to destroy free will and its expression at the polls of the people of Manitoba in three specified constituencies. How far this was the method generally adopted, who can say?
I have not time to go through the correspondence; I wish simply to bring home some outstanding points. Looking at the order in council, and its date in relation to this earlier correspondence, the whole story is there, as complete as it can be-an order put through on the eve of an election, just for the purpose of letting these poor people who were then so hard pressed in the province of Manitoba- starving, many of them, as the right hon. the leader of the opposition would say- believe that at last help was coming from the public treasury.
And the work was to be there by the tenth of October.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
And the work was to be there, and all would be well. But in the back of the minds of all these gentlemen there was the knowledge or intention that as soon as the election was over-no more work- whether the people starved or did not starve.
I say that in all Canadian history there has never been an exposure of corruption and corrupt political methods so disgraceful.
Read this! Beauharnoisl Beauharnois! Read that.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Beauharnois is a shadow compared with this thing. The right hon. the leader of the opposition comes along and shouts, " Beauharnois " 1 And after all his talk about Beauharnois, he sits in a cabinet and as Prime Minister does something that is infinitely worse than anything ever done by any of those connected with Beauharnois, more than anything that was done by men who were not even members of the House of Commons.
Quite; and neither was Webb.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, but my right hon. friend was Prime Minister.
And so were you!

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
But I had
not any knowledge of the evils my right hon. friend speaks about.

The record shows you
had.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, I had not, and my right hon. friend knows it. He himself was the engineer in this whole business. He sent directions as to what should be done over the head of his own minister, telling what was to be done.

As a matter of fact, it
does not say in the telegram what he was to do.

Why did you send it,
then?
He intimated to me that it had been received from the Minister of the Interior. The record is there, and I say the Prime Minister is bound by it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right
hon. friend has spoken about Beauharnois.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He talks
about Beauharnois in this house, and he talked about Beauharnois across this country from coast to coast, with what results? With the result that he came back to this parliament with his party defeated, with his party emasculated, well-nigh annihilated, and without a following behind him worthy of the name, leaving some of the provinces of this country without a single Conservative member, and with what further result? The Conservative party is not only obliterated for the time being, but, as we saw by the election two days ago, is obliterated possibly for all time as a party. And what at the same time was the verdict, with respect to myself, by the people of this country? The man whom he sought to condemn is sent back to this parliament with the largest following any leader of a political party or any Prime Minister in Canada has ever had. I tell my right hon. friend that for what has been disclosed to-day the people of this country will pass judgment upon him some day.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
With respect
to this matter he will get out of all this before judgment is passed in this house; but let me tell him that the judgment which will follow him is the record of this House of Commons of to-day; the record of his own words will follow him for the remainder of his term in this house; they will follow him

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
to the end of his days, and they will remain a judgment against him as long as a record of this parliament remains.
I assume this house is still discussing item No. 103, is that right?
Item No. 108.

There were certain items discussed during the course of this afternoon that did not create a very gratifying reflection upon the present government. I notice that whenever a person or a government is confronted with a difficult proposition, it attempts to cover up by the throwing of mud, and the raking up of past history. I do not see that what the Prime Minister has said to-night, or the snickering grin and laughter of the Minister of National Defence-
Thank you.
-in any way eradicates the suggestion that was made from the opposition benches this afternoon in connection with the work that is being done in and around the city of Kingston.
Hear, hear.
It was my privilege to visit- Mr. BENNETT: The commandant's report. Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver): I have it here.
-my native city last weekend. I want to say to the committee that it is common gossip on the streets of Kingston-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: "Gossip" is right.

Yes, gossip is right. And I want to say this in passing, to the Minister of National Defence, that when the opportunity comes to look into the details of his department we shall then be able to see to what extent political debauchery and corruption have crept into that particular department of government.
Do it now.
No; that item is not before the committee.
It is not possible to do it now, but the time will come when we shall look into it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
I shall come back to the city of Kingston.
You had better.
I can go there with my head in the air, and be respected by the citizens of the city of Kingston. I was saying that it is common gossip-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, gossip.

I was saying that it is street gossip, everyone is talking about it in the city of Kingston, as to what is being done in connection with public works there. I want to say this in passing, that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) personally is not in any way being blamed for the condition that has arisen there.
Blame your leader.
I say that in all fairness.
You cannot be fair.

I could not be fair with some people, because some people do not know what the word "fair" actually means. I do not consider that the Minister of Labour himself has in any way connived at what has developed there. Unfortunately, what has developed is the creature of our political system. The sooner the two major parties and the two minor parties of this house get together as public-spirited men and women, the sooner shall we eradicate this sort of business from the political life of our country. As I sat here and listened to what one government was said to have done in the past, and to what another government was said to be doing at the present time, I wondered what the people of Canada were going to think when they read their daily newspaper tomorrow morning or to-morrow evening. The reflection that has been cast upon democracy as it exists in Canada to-day is not at all gratifying. For this government to sit here and suggest that they are doing these things because it was done to an even greater extent in the past-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That was never suggested by anybody.

Why rake up past history? Why go into old history to bolster up what I consider to be a rather weak case? The question before the committee is a serious one as far as public life is concerned. The right hon. Prime Minister boasts of a very large following. Fortunately for him and for his party they are the creatures of peculiar circumstances. He takes credit for the great victory achieved by the Liberal party in 1935. Any person with any degree of knowledge of past political history will be able to analyse the situation that developed in 1935 and made it almost impossible for any other action to be taken by the Canadian people. From 1930 to

1935 this country was governed by a leader and a government who did everything in their power to remedy a serious condition. During that time they received little or no assistance from those sitting in opposition. The country went through a difficult period, and if we analyse the conditions of that time we can see readily how the people had not the time prior to 1935 to appreciate what had actually been done by the government which was in office from 1930 to 1935.
What about Saskatchewan?

I do not think the Liberal members can take a great deal of real satisfaction out of the victory in Saskatchewan. If you will have written on the records of Hansard; if you will have published and broadcast from one end of Canada to the other exactly what did take place in Saskatchewan, I can assure you that the people will be more disgusted with that phase of democratic government than they will with what exists here in Ottawa at the present time. Everything that was possible to be used was used in Saskatchewan.
Does my hon. friend not agree with the decision of Saskatchewan?
I do not agree with the conditions that brought about the decision in Saskatchewan. Any one who does agree with those conditions has no right to continue in public life.
What are the conditions with which you do not agree?
You are more familiar with them than I. I have an idea of what took place out there, but it is not as good an idea as my hon. friend's.
Does my hon. friend agree with what happened in Manitoba prior to the 1935 election?
I want to come back to this discussion. The Liberal party has complained of third parties in the field.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Never.
The more the merrier.

You have complained of the "more," but not of the "merrier." There is every ^ reason to expect third parties in the field in Canada, and fourth parties as well.
If conditions in public life, as exemplified by the statements of the leader of the opposition and the Prime Minister, are allowed to continue unremedied, the people of this country are bound to ask for a different form of government. If any member of this house is

interested in the survival of democracy in Canada, he will not aid and abet what has taken place and what is taking place in our public offices, but will make a serious endeavour to clean the slate, start over again and give democracy a real chance. I do not see why we cannot be businesslike in the expenditure of public moneys. I do not see why we cannot expend public money just as we expend our private funds. I do not see any reason why there should be a suggestion in this house that there is a conspiracy to give only Liberals jobs when a Liberal government is in power.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We cannot prevent you from saying that. That is the trouble; you say it whether it is true or not.

I would not say it if it did not exist. I started out like the Minister of Labour. I was in an academic institution, and during the course of my campaign in 1935 I gave utterance to words very similar to those uttered by the minister. I had my high ideals and, like him, I still have them. I hope I am going to be able to maintain them despite what I have had to listen to in this chamber during the course of this evening and this afternoon. If we had less laughter from the treasury benches and more serious contemplation of what is taking place in government circles, this matter would be remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What we want is more truth in opposition statements.

There are several points that could be brought up, but I see no reason for doing so. I think this matter has been emphasized sufficiently, and I feel sure that members of the house have come to the realization that something must be done in order to prevent a continuation of a practice that apparently has grown up and rooted itself in our democracy. This practice does not belong there. I feel quite sure that the Minister of Labour will be among the first to make an effort to eradicate this system, root and all. I have sufficient confidence in the Prime Minister and in those associated with him to feel that they are ready to assist this country out of the quagmire in which it is at present. It is unfortunate that this discussion has developed. It is unfortunate that we have had to refer to conditions that exist in Kingston. I do not associate those conditions with the Minister of Labour, but I do associate them with what we have allowed to grow up. As parliamentarians we ought to be bigger men. We should rise up in firm

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
determination to eliminate these conditions from the public life of Canada so that the people may have their faith reestablished in the democratic form of government that exists in Canada to-day.

I assure members of the committee that no one deplores more than I do that two full days should have been occupied in the kind of discussion we have had here. I am in the judgment of the committee when I say that, in view of the statements made on several occasions by the leader of the opposition, I had no recourse but to meet those charges, and my colleagues had no recourse but to meet such charges. My hon. friend who has just spoken has expressed the view that as Minister of Labour I have a certain sense of obligation with respect to the duties of my office. I hope I have.
When the leader of the opposition first brought these matters to the attention of the house, I asked him to let me have any complaints which he might have received, and said that I would take the earliest opportunity of dealing with them. He referred specifically to Fort Henry, and he certainly designedly created the impression that no one but a Liberal could secure employment on the work at Fort Henry. I told him without the slightest hesitation some days ago that in my view, on relief work which is done in cooperation with the provinces, for which money is paid out of relief votes of this parliament, there should not be discrimination, and that whenever I received complaints of discrimination they were investigated without the slightest delay. My right hon. friend simply made the statement, that so far as he understood-he occasionally admitted that his recollection was faulty-none but Liberals would receive employment on the work at Fort Henry.
He did not say that.
I beg the right hon. gentleman's pardon.
He did not say that.

Well, that was certainly
the implication of what my right hon. friend said.
He did not say that. [DOT]

I shall look up Hansard to correct that impression if it is incorrect. Immediately after that, I wrote to the Frid Construction Company, which had the contract for that work at Fort Henry, and I also wrote to the chief relief officer in the
city of Kingston. I received first from the chief relief officer in the city of Kingston this letter; it is from Colonel Pense:
I have spoken to Mr. J. K. Fraser, chairman of the social welfare committee, in regard to your letter of the 16th instant.
There is no hesitation in saying that no political considerations have ever entered into the administration of the social welfare department of Kingston; any names that have been submitted to the employment office were submitted without regard to any political affiliations the person might, or might not, have.
The letter from the Frid Construction Company is in the following terms:
Your letter re selecting applicants for employment on our contract at Fort Henry duly received, and I am glad of the opportunity of explaining this to you.
The clause re labour in our contract stated that our company was allowed to employ twenty-five per cent of our own men. The other seventy-five per cent we were obliged to take through the government employment office in Kingston.
From the beginning when men were required we called the employment office, and these men were all sent to us with an employment office card. These men as far as our superintendent was concerned were never asked as to their political affiliations. We required only that the men employed must be able to perform their work in a satisfactory manner, otherwise they were paid off.
Regarding the twenty-five per cent which we were allowed to hire ourselves. They of course were of our own selecting, mostly foreman, clerks and skilled workmen. In each case we naturally picked the best men available for the different positions.
It has never been the policy of our company either on this or any other job, to ask the employees questions pertaining to their political affiliations or religious beliefs. In every case the prime requisite for employees is their ability to handle work well and efficiently.
In one or two cases only, men were recommended to us by friends, and we did see they got work under our twenty-five per cent quota, and if they turned out to be good men we kept them on.
I am enclosing some private correspondence I had regarding these workmen for your information.
I am reluctant to mention these few cases as the men given employment were heads of families and in very dire straits, and we did feel justified in doing this, as their employment meant so little when compared to the total number of men employed.
Our company has carried out the labour part of our agreement very carefully and we believe to the satisfaction of Mr. Hudson who is general superintendent, Ontario government office, employment service of Canada. I am enclosing letter we received from him under date of April 14, 1937, which speaks for itself.
In that enclosure the head of the Frid Construction Company does acknowledge that he did receive certain recommendations from

a member of parliament, and I think I should say that to the members of the committee. Does the leader of the opposition feel there was anything out of the way in that?
Not the slightest-
I am glad that he does not.
-because the contract provides that the head of this company is to have his own foremen and that he is to get the balance of the labour under the Ontario employment commission.
Precisely.
And it is because the head of the Ontario employment commission took the position he did, as I indicated yesterday, that I complained. I never complained about the Frid Construction Company.

I am entirely in agreement with that statement, because the only letter he received from a member of parliament was from a member on the opposition side. And I may say that two and possibly three men were placed because of requests made by one of the friends of my right hon. friend. I should also say this, that two of the subcontracts on the work at Fort Henry were given to Conservatives in Kingston, and those actively in charge of the work are members of the Conservative association in the city of Kingston and control entirely the employees whom they use on that part of the work.
My right hon. friend complained this afternoon of the cost of the work at Fort Henry. He said it had already reached close to a million.
I said it was nearer a million than seventy thousand.
Well, that is correct, but my right hon. friend allowed himself considerable latitude in making that statement.
That is exactly what he said.
That is quite correct. That is the statement he made, that it was nearer a million than seventy thousand, but certainly the inference was that it was a gigantic expenditure.
I said that it was several hundred thousand dollars.

Strictly, up to date the expenditure has been $498,000, of which the dominion government has contributed one-half, which is under $250,000. I gave the committee this afternoon the conditions respecting the tenders which were invited for that work. I might say that in each year, 
1936 and 1937, tenders were publicly advertised, advertised in the public journals, in the Globe and Mail, and in certain trade papers.
Could the hon. gentleman give me a little information respecting that? I have a copy of the specifications respecting the first tender, June 30, 1936. Can he fix the date of the second?

My information is that the second tender was awarded in March, 1937. The first tender was for $72,000. The work was actually extended beyond that on the same unit prices, as I explained this afternoon. The second tender was for $305,000. That is the information I have.
Were tenders called for the second contract?
Tenders were called for the second contract.
Public tenders?
Public tenders, yes.
I have not a copy of these specifications.

I am giving my information. My right hon. friend also went on to say this afternoon that in connection with the disposal of certain huts which were left when the relief camps were closed, there had been irregularities.
Not huts. I said-

Equipment. These are his words:
There were two camps in and around Kingston. Camp 42 was one and camp 37 was the other. Both camps were closed by the government. There was much clothing and supplies in one of those camps. They were placed in a storeroom. They were sold. And in a public meeting one of the electors of Kingston, at Sydenham, gave illustrations as to the prices received for them and the method of their disposition-horses, wagons and costly equipment. Who got it, and at what price? And it is a singular coincidence that within four hours after the conclusion of that speech at Sydenham the storehouse was on fire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is what he said.
Yes; that is what I said.

Well, certainly my right hon. friend must have had it in his mind to create some impression by his statement. I am bound to say that after reading that statement I am not yet clear as to what precisely he had in mind. Actually the disposal of the equipment of the relief camps was undertaken by the salvage officer of the dominion government. The huts themselves, as I explained previously to the committee, were not given to friends of the administration

in power; they were disposed of at a nominal price to various welfare organizations. I have a list of them here, if my right hon. friend desires them.
I made no observations about the huts.

As to the fire, my information is that the fire occurred in a hut which was used for storage purposes by the signal corps at Barriefield. The contents of the hut were fully insured and the insurance was paid. That is my information at the present time. Obviously, therefore, there is nothing whatever in that statement. My right hon. friend also made some charge with respect to the movement of cement from one contract held by the Frid Construction Company to another contract held by the same company in the city of Kingston. Here again I have lost no time in securing information, and if he had written me a letter I could have given him the information within twenty-four hours and saved the time of the house by doing so. The cement for the Crain building, which is being constructed at Queen's, was borrowed from the Fort Henry job with the consent of the provincial authorities, and it was returned to that job on the following dates: November 1, 1,000 bags; January 17, 750 bags.
Why were the empty bags taken to Fort Henry?

My information is that talk about the returning of empty bags to Fort Henry is utter rot; that is the memorandum I have. It reads:
The talk about returning the empty bags to Fort Henry from Crain building is utter rot. In the old days when cement was put up in canvas sacks they were returnable and had a value. For quite a few years the department of highways has been purchasing its cement, as do most users, in paper bags which are not returnable. The cement referred to in two items above was ordered by Frid, charged to Crain job and then transferred to the Fort job.
I made it perfectly clear that they were paper sacks.
So that there is nothing left of that charge.
Were they sent up there at night, and if so, for what purpose?
My right hon. friend is confusing his charges. The cement was not taken at night.
I did not say that; I said the bags.
My right hon. friend said that twenty-five containers of white lead were taken after midnight.
That is not cement.
Well, the committee will pardon me if I confuse the cement, white lead, cut stone and various other materials-
Cut flowers and cast-iron pipe.

-that have been brought into the discussion; but up to the present time I have not been able to discover that there have been at any time on the Fort Henry job or at camp 42 as many as twenty-five containers of white lead. My information is that at camp 42 there had never been more than one or two cans of white lead required for their purpose, and not more than one can had been required for work at Fort Henry. What, therefore, is left of that charge, I confess I do not know. I have tried to get the information, and that is as much as I have at the present time.
My right hon. friend also had something to say about some stone which apparently had gone in some clandestine way from the Royal Military College to the grounds of Mr. Stans-bury. Again, to the best of my ability, I have not been able to discover the slightest scintilla of evidence which would support that charge. I dealt this afternoon with his first charge, that Mr. Stansbury had built his garage from public property, and my strong conviction is that there is just about as much foundation for his second charge as there was for his first. My right hon. friend, in speaking of the way in which he dealt with employment, said that in Calgary the names were put into a hat and drawn from the hat. Am I correct?
That is what I was told; I was not there.
Oh, oh.
Everyone knows that I was not in Calgary. The mayor told me that was the way in which it was dealt with.

I do not think it is unfair to suggest that it would have been a very good thing if that hat had been preserved in some way, because it was the only hat used for that purpose when my right hon. friend was in power. However, I will read a letter which was sent to the leader of the opposition on May 23, 1935, from Charles E. Scott, recording secretary of local No. 1779 of the Carpenters and Joiners of America.

Has the minister any
idea when the letter was received?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It was a letter that came to me when I was leader of the opposition. It was sent by the union. It was

sent by the carpenters' union when I was in the position now occupied by the leader of the opposition. It stated what was taking place in Calgary in the matter of giving employment to men, and the letter was put on Hansard at tihe time.
To whom is it addressed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was then
leader of the opposition and it was addressed to me as such.

The letter refers to the
barracks then being built at Calgary under the Department of National Defence.
The minister said that it was addressed to me.
I correct that statement; it was addressed to the present Prime Minister When he was leader of the opposition. That, of course, need not affect the subject matter of the letter.
Not a bit.

The letter reads:
The members of the above local wish to inform you that when the building of the barracks at Calgary was announced it was generally accepted that the available work would be spread out to afford a maximum of assistance to the various classes of craftsmen which it might employ.
Contractors opened lists for the carpenters who had worked for them at various periods, and many workmen hoped that after waiting many months for the work to begin that at least they would be able to get a few days' employment. Now we are to understand that the only hope of ever getting work on the barracks job is when his name is on the approved list which is furnished to the contractors.
The members of Local No. 1779 request that when parliament is opened a protest be vigorously made against the practice of using this patronage list, as it is debarring carpenters who are loyal and have been citizens of this country for the last twenty-five to thirty years, also a large percentage of the members being ex-service men. Owing to this approved list being used certain carpenters are being given employment by the various contractors on the scheme, thereby making it impossible for others to get employment.
Trusting you will give this appeal your greatest consideration.
Yours truly,
per Charles E. Scott,
Recording Secretary.
What was the date of it?
It is in Hansard of May 23, 1935. It will be found at page 3035. Now, in view of my right hon. friend's statement yesterday, surely he will agree that there is a sharp contradiction-
Not in the least. The list furnished was the list provided by drawings from the hat. That is exactly what happened.
I am content to read the letter again, but that is what I might regard as an extremely forced construction of the letter as it stands.
I was not there, but tire mayor told me that that was how they brought peace and harmony into the field.
So far as I am concerned-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My right hon. friend did not say that it was the mayor. What he said was:
In my own community I know that effect was given to that endeavour by putting the names in a hat and having them drawn.
I know from the mayor's statement that he did it. That is sufficient for my purpose.
Why is not the hat produced as evidence?

In conclusion, may I say that with regard to employment at the present time I propose to continue to see, so far as in me lies, that when that work is conducted as relief work we shall obtain the strictest observance possible of the clause with respect to discrimination.
As far as other casual vacancies which become available from time to time are concerned, if these are to be taken under the control of the civil service commission, well and good; but if they are not, I do not hesitate to take responsibility as a member of parliament for any recommendations which I make. I am not prepared to say whether or not that is the best course finally to follow. But in conclusion I would suggest that a great deal of this debate, perhaps all of it, could have been avoided if my right hon. friend, instead of accepting these rumours and suspicions and gossip which came to him from sources which I think I know in Kingston-which gossip and rumours he made no real effort to corroborate before bringing to this committee-had made an effort to test the truth of them, or had brought them to the attention of the department best fitted to deal with them, he would have rendered a far greater service to the country than he did yesterday and this afternoon.

Having
been mentioned this afternoon and again this evening by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), it is my desire now to refer to three

I have here a departmental memorandum which describes in the fullest and most complete way all the transactions that took place at Barriefield, and apart from what was mentioned by my colleague, that most of the equipment there was given to charitable institutions, I find that two sales were made from project 37 through the salvage officer, who is an officer of this government, and who was not a member of the Department of National Defence. This committee heard this afternoon certain suggestions made with reference to horses, etc. The official departmental memorandum is as follows:
In September 1937 representations were received to the effect that certain stores and equipment, that is, cement, paint, and Bain wagons, were given Or sold at inadequate prices to neighbouring farmers. The matter was investigated. The report received indicated that the only Bain wagons used at project 42 were privately-owned and were brought in with hired teams of horses; also that there were no shortages in stores, including paint or cement.
With respect to this alarming fire with which the right hon. gentleman tried to stir up the waning enthusiasm of his miserable remnant over there-

A matter of order, Mr. Chairman. The hon. member is very apt at that sort of thing to-day. But he cannot call any hon. members of this chamber miserable remnants. The rule is very clear on that point.
Well, if the remark is in the slighest degree unpleasant, I have the greatest pleasure in withdrawing it.	.
No, I rise again to a point of order.

I have withdrawn it. With respect to this fire, this sinister fire, in the cold hours of the angry dawn, about which the right hon. gentleman was endeavouring to stir up a tremendous suspicion, I wish to tell the committee that a most thorough investigation was held by the Department of National Defence, and no blame was found attributable to any individual. A meeting took place, and four hours after the meeting a fire. Hence this scandal referred to this afternoon by the right hon. gentleman.
Now we have something still worse. Where does all this tittle-tattle come from? Where does this street gossip of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Walsh) come from? I think I know. And I am going to tell. The other afternoon in the house, referring to a tender of the Department of National Defence the right hon. leader of the opposition made this accusation: He said we did not give the contract to the lowest bidder, and so lost thousands of dollars to the country. Well, I want to tell the committee something about the gentleman whom the right hon. leader of the opposition was defending. I had some evidence before me; it was not 'of a political nature I can assure my right hon. friend; but his information has been derived from a gentleman concerning whom I shall read an affidavit, showing that he was guilty of the most vicious malpractice with reference to contracts with the government of Ontario. Possessing that knowledge which came to me as a responsible minister, I refused, and instructed my deputy minister to refuse, to allow the contract to go to that gentleman. Why? This is not street gossip. This is an affidavit of Alfred Leonard Gibson of the village of Kemptville in the county of Grenville, superintendent:
1.	I am superintendent of the Eastern Dairy School of the Ontario Department of Agriculture.
2.	The Eastern Dairy School was carried on at Kingston, Ontario, until April, 1936.

During the period August 1, 1932, to July 31, 1933, coal was supplied to the said school by Sowards Coal Company of Kingston, Ontario, at the price of $6.50 per ton, four deliveries of coal having been made during that period; the amounts of the deliveries being 63 tons, 1,060 lbs.; 63 tons. 1,303 lbs.; 63 tons, 1,410 lbs.; and 55 tons, 250 lbs. respectively, the total cost for the period being $1,599.08.

And I make this solemn declaration conscientiously believing it to be true . . .
The declaration, was sworn before George J. Mcllraith on June 4, 1938.
I want to reiterate the essential portion of that declaration. During the winters of 1931-32, 1932-33 and 1933-34 the average cost of coal purchased per annum was $1,422. All these purchases were made from the James Sowards Coal Company of Kingston, at a price of $6.50 per ton for all the coal with the exception of one small order of forty-one tons at $7 a ton. For the winters of 1934-35 and 1935-36 the average cost for coal for the same institution was $854. This coal was purchased not from the Sowards coal company but from another Kingston company which supplied coal at $7 a ton.

What was the name of
the firm?

So I ask the committee to consider this; If it cost that institution $1,422 per annum for its fuel requirements when dealing with one company, and $854 per annum when dealing with another company at a higher price per ton, if you please, certainly to me it would appear quite obvious that it was not in the public interest to deal with a company like the Sowards company in any part of the Dominion of Canada. The one who is the chief informer in regard to the comedy we have witnesed during the last two days, who has been endeavouring to shove sixty-three tons of coal into a fifty-ton storage bin, does not deserve the support of any self-respecting minister of the crown in Canada.
I come now to something else. Did you hear these sinister, subterranean, surreptitious whispers this afternoon about a report

that was made by the commandant of the Royal Military College at Kingston, some report dealing with rock, some mysterious rock that disappeared in the night? I asked one of the highest ranking militia officers in the department-not my deputy minister-to telephone the commandant of the Royal Military College with reference to this report; and, Mr. Chairman, there is no report. It was all a fabrication; it was all imagination, a dream on the part of the right hon. gentleman.
At last.
I want now to deal with the hon. member for Mount Royal, who made the statement a few minutes ago that there was debauchery-I think that was the word he used-in the Department of National Defence.
For want of a better term.

I want to tell my hon. friend right now that he has certain duties and obligations in this house, and if he knows anything against the honour or integrity of the minister or any officer of this department let him have enough manliness to rise in his place now, make a charge and place his seat in jeopardy, as a gentleman of honour, with reference to these rumours he has been pretending to tell about.
Would the minister permit me to suggest-

I think I am in order, Mr. Chairman. I cannot imagine anything more despicable than such action on the part of any hon. gentleman. I might remind the hon. member that at the commencement of this session I offered the right hon. leader of the opposition the hon. gentlemen opposite the opportunity, by a special resolution of this house, to call together the public accounts committee one year in advance of the time that is fixed by parliament, in order to investigate any single feature of any of the business of the Department of National Defence. What did they do? They refused that offer, but now the hon. member for Mount Royal rises in his place and talks about debauchery and something else. Will my hon. friend follow that up? Will he do it now? I challenge him; I dare him; I defy him to do it now, instead of slinking in his seat, skulking in his place. Let him do it like a man; let him place his seat in jeopardy and make some specific charge with reference to the Department of National Defence. For two days now, Mr. Chairman, we have listened to these sinister

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
rumours. Why, if we wanted to recall what occurred between 1930 and 1935, what could we say? I know what happened in Calgary; I know what happened in Vancouver; I know what happened in the relief camps of British Columbia; and I think I know now, for the first time, what happened to " my dear chief " in Manitoba.
However, the business of the country must be carried on, despite these unfortunate interruptions; and the right hon. leader of the opposition never did himself less justice than he did this afternoon. According at least to the accepted rumours in the journals of the country, this gentleman of great experience, who has been Prime Minister of this great nation, is leaving public life. He should have gone out with the halo of public esteem about his head; but he has misspent the last two days in imputing motives, repeating petty rumours about some stone that cost two or three dollars, while on the other hand a letter was read from the mayor of Winnipeg, the director of the Conservative party in Manitoba, involving a total expenditure of $1,365,000. Waking up at last.

A few weeks ago we received a lecture on political morality and corruption across Canada. We did not know then what he and his esteemed colleagues had in mind. I was interested to hear the name of Hon. Mr. Manion mentioned, a gentleman who occupied a cabinet post in the last administration. I have no doubt that the receipt by that gentleman of the letter which the Prime Minister also received, and his participation in the contribution of $1,365,000 to buy three seats in Manitoba, will commend that gentleman to his colleagues in this house at the coming convention. At least he is not stingy in spending public money to buy the voters in elections. If I read the judgment of the people of Canada aright, he is going to have to raise the ante if he is to be accorded the leadership of the party; and he is going to have to exceed the $355,000 per seat in order to endeavour to fool the people some of the time.
After the lessons in political morality and on the evils of corruption that we have received, the right hon. gentleman has spent this afternoon in what I think is the most grotesque exhibition that it has been my privilege to witness since I have been in this House of Commons.
