We have a migration of young women as well as young men to the coast. Many of these young women register with the employment service. They are sent out by the officials of the service to various employment opportunities as reported to the offices. At one stage apparently no endeavour was made to check those reported openings in order to protect these young women against victimization. I was taken to task on one occasion by a gentleman who was then attorney general of British Columbia for mentioning the recruiting for a chain of brothels in British Columbia. I am not concerned at the moment about proving whether or not brothels exist, or in discussing law enforcement in British Columbia; but it is known to all who are interested in public affairs at the coast that a certain degree of recruiting does go on. I am asking the minister to explain to the committee to what extent facilities have been developed so that these opportunities are checked by some follow-up protection, in order that young women placed through the employment service are adequately protected

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
against exploitation either by those who seek to take advantage of their destitution by imposing low wages, sweat-shop conditions, or against actual victimization by agents of the underworld.

When my hon. friend
raised this point before six o'clock I did not recall the discussion of a year ago. I do recall it now. I am not at present able to give my hon. friend the information for which he has asked. I did leave word for communication to be made with the director of the employment service there to see what action had been taken, after the discussion of last year. I have not that information yet, but will secure it as soon as possible.

In the discussions we have had during the last three or four weeks in regard to the single unemployed in Vancouver, the minister, if I understood him aright, has taken the position that employment is available in British Columbia. I do not know exactly what the situation may be to-day; possibly the minister has the information; but I have the May issue of the Labour Gazette, and I find that there were almost 10,000 registrations at the labour offices in British Columbia during March, and that there were only 2,518 placements. As a matter of fact, about one-third of the placements are for a duration of around one week, and the remainder for longer periods of time. At the end of March there were over 13,000 unplaced who had registered for work. In the face of figures such as those, how can the minister take the position that the unemployed in Vancouver at the present time can find work?

My information is that last year in British Columbia the placements were as follows:
Men Women
In regular work	
18,786	3,574In casual work	
26,109	3,902
Total placements in British
Columbia	 52,371
At any given time, as my hon. friend is aware, the applications for employment would exceed the placements. But it does not follow-and it was this point I endeavoured to make yesterday-that all placements in British Columbia or any other province are obtained through the facilities of the employment service of Canada. So I do not think the figures given by my hon. friend are conclusive in that regard.

They may not be conclusive, but they are just as conclusive as the figures given by the Minister of Labour. I
have here the figures for March of this year. There was a decline of nearly thirty-four per cent in the number of positions offered through the employment offices in British Columbia. Would the minister say that this would not have any effect on the number of positions offering in the labour market generally in British Columbia? Is it not to be supposed that when there is a decline in the number of positions offered through the labour offices there is likely to be a corresponding decline in the number of positions offered in other ways? I say again that the position taken by the minister in regard to the situation in Vancouver and British Columbia, where men are unable to get work and are refused relief, is not at all in accord with the high sentiments we heard expressed this afternoon. I ask again that the minister take the situation under his consideration and see whether something cannot be done immediately to avoid the trouble which will undoubtedly take place there unless something is done.
Is the Ottawa office of the department represented in Vancouver at the present time? If so, who is the individual representing the department there in regard to the situation?

In regard to the situation which has been under discussion from time to time in the last few weeks, the representative of the department who has been in Vancouver is Mr. Humphrey Mitchell, who has been director of labour transference in the department during the last two and a half years.
Is he an officer of the employment service?
He is not an officer of the employment service.

What is his standing
within the service?
He is a temporary employee of the department, appointed under the Unemployment and Agricultural Distress Act of 1936.
What is the salary in connection with that position?
It does not come under this item, but it is $500 a month.

The item under consideration involves payments to the labour employment service maintained in several provinces and at various points in many provinces. During the progress of the discussion, the minister made a statement with respect to the item,
3758	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
in reply to a question as to how that office was conducted in the city of Kingston, which is operated by a man named Mooers; I think that is the way it is spelled.
That is correct.

I presented to this committee, as was my duty, evidence that indicated his complete unfitness for that position; and I read from a public print that reference had been made to his practically holding up people for contributions to his beer fund or liquor fund in order that they might find employment. I did more; I produced a letter from a reputable person who had gone to that office for the purpose of securing employment and had been sent to the president of the Liberal association, or told that without the approval of the president of the Liberal association he could not find employment. I followed that by saying that Mr. Stansbury did in fact give him a letter to the Frontenac Construction Company-
He did what he could to secure employment for him.

-to secure him a job, and that it was laughed at. That involved the conduct of the man in charge of this office in Kingston, and I say to the minister that the evidence completely establishes the man's unfitness for his position. It is true that he was not appointed by this government. He was appointed by the provincial administration, and I pointed out to the minister that under those circumstances such a man was not a fit and proper person to be charged with that responsibility. I also referred to a contract, because during the course of his statement the minister said that conditions were inserted in the contracts for tenders which made it incumbent upon those who sought additional labour on contracts to get it from this body or through this office. The language in the bids for the Fort Henry property is as follows:
Contractors may use machinery, wherever desired.
The men selected by the Department of Labour shall not be rotated on the job, and may be dismissed if their services are not satisfactory. A written statement shall be supplied to the representative of the Department of Labour, indicating the reason for dismissal, in each individual case, and contractors are urged to give men a second chance, if they fail to make good on the job for which they were originally selected.
That follows the conditions that are to prevail with respect to the hiring of labour:
All labour to be supplied on these contracts shall be supplied through the Ontario Department of Labour. Contractors will be permitted, however, to supply such men as are required 	.
for supervision, and special work approved by the department, but the number of men so engaged by the contractors shall not exceed fifteen per cent of the total number on the job.
That was later changed to twenty-five per cent.

I am only reading from the bid that was circulated, because it is only fair to point out that with respect to the Fort Henry job it was through the department of highways of Ontario that tenders were asked, and the tenders called for indicated that a certain defined work as mentioned in the plan was the work to which the contractor was to direct his attention. I find nowhere a provision such as would constitute any safeguard for the dominion in that bid. There may be in some bids, or there may be in the final contract, but in this bid so far as I can see-and the typewritten portion with respect to labour is made separate -there is no provision to safeguard that position.
I do say to the minister, to the hon. member for Parry Sound and to the hon. gentlemen on the treasury benches, that we should not have the taxpayers of Canada providing half the cost of this undertaking and have the control of the labour in the hands of a man of the type that the evidence indicates he was and is. No one for a moment has suggested that any statement made with respect to him is not true. No one has risen in his defence, not even the hon. member for Parry Sound. No one has said that he was attacked behind his back.
Surely the charges of my hon. friend are charges which ought to be and which will be investigated.

My point was that the investigation should have been made long ago, because this, in the language of the great apostle, was not done in a corner. The hon. member for Parry Sound says it is street gossip; but it is more than that; it reaches the public press in a case that is tried in the police court.
If my right hon. friend will permit me, he has made certain definite statements with respect to the present officer in charge of the employment service in Kingston.
I quoted from documents.

But those statements
certainly did not go to show in any way that Mr. Mooers has used his position in such a way as to discriminate wholly in favour of Liberals and against Conservatives. I do not believe there is any basis for that charge in what my right hon. friend has said.

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
I read a letter from a reputable citizen of Kingston who went there for employment.
Yes, one person.
But there can be others secured, as I told the hon. gentleman. This man was told, "You will have to have a letter from the president of the Liberal association."
Not for relief work at all.
Well, I gathered that part of the Fort Henry work was treated as a relief job.
This was at Barriefield.

Rollands heard there was a vacancy at Barriefield, but he wanted a job anywhere. Let us have no misunderstanding about it; that is the position. I have another letter here, which is signed by Mr. J. Marshall, rural route No. 1, Kingston, Ontario, dated May 10, 1938, which is not very long ago:
Sir:
A few lines hoping to be excused. I have been asking Mr. Rogers for a job for the past fifteen months but all he tells me to keep in touch with Mr. Stansberry. I have seen him several times but all he tells me their is nothing doing. I cooked in camp 42 for over two years and as not be able to get very much since I hope that you will try and get me a job as it is very hard for me to give without working.
Hoping to hear from you soon,
Yours truly,
J. Marshall.
I do not know who he is.

If my right hon. friend
will permit me, I did not know the other people to whom he referred, but I do recall Mr. Marshall. He has applied to me for a position; he has written to me on various occasions. I believe at one time he was a cook attached either to camp 42 or camp 37. I have not the slightest idea what his political affiliations are.
Was he referred to Mr. Stansbury?

If he says so, I would
not deny it, for this reason:	When I go
back to Kingston I am approached by men who ask for jobs. I have had to leave with my local executive such contact with such openings as do occur in Kingston.
Quite.

That I have said quite
frankly in the house at various times.

But it negatives a statement which the minister made in the heat
of the argument this afternoon, that there were no cases in which he had referred anyone to Stansbury.

No, no, I did not say
that.

What he is saying now
I have followed. What he said this afternoon is at variance with that, perhaps because he was dealing with another phase of the same matter.

I never referred anyone,
or spoke to a contractor in Kingston in favour of any person, or instructed anyone else to do so.

I am not discussing that phase of the matter. I am talking about the question of the minister referring this man to the president of the Liberal association for the purpose of getting a position. That at least is evidence of that phase of it.
Now comes the hon. member for Parry Sound who says, "You are casting a reflection upon Stansbury, upon Rigney, upon Shea and upon a salvage officer because their names are discussed in this house." Well, the other evening the Minister of National Defence, a minister of the crown, when speaking of the Sowards incident, he having submitted the lowest tender for coal, and when I had asked him about the reports received concerning the firm, and to quote the language of the order in council, used these words:
I have not the documents before me at the moment with reference to the particular tender mentioned by the right hon. gentleman, but I definitely recall that complaints were made in regard to the carrying out of a previous contract by this same gentleman, with reference to a definite breach of the labour conditions in the contract. I shall ascertain the exact terms of the complaint and shall be glad to supply it to my right hon. friend or to any member of the committee.
This evening there was read a statutory declaration dated June 4, 1938, a week ago to-morrow. And the order in council was pased in 1937. What does he mean?
Nothing; I just meant-
"Nothing," I thought so.

It is all very well to be clever. The information was given me at the time. I did not have it in my recollection at the time, and the information was given to me by my colleague the Minister of Labour, and was substantiated to-night.

That is right. Had I
been in the house at the time I would not
3760	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
have hesitated for a moment to say that I had sent on the information. The information was not at that time in the form of a statutory declaration. But when I noted the manner in which it was regarded by the leader of the opposition I thought he would appreciate it more perhaps if it was in the form of a sworn statement.

It is Mr. Gibson who
gave the statutory declaration of June 4, which reduced into writing what had prevously been ascertained. But Mr. Gibson is a cheese-maker; he is a dairy inspector.

And a very capable man,
and the superintendent of a school.

Yes, a very capable
man and the superintendent of a school. Since when did a competent cheese-maker become equipped to tell the number of tons of coal a bin would hold?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
A high-school boy can
do that.
I will say to the Minister of Finance that it depends entirely on the kind of coal.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Exactly, yes.

Well, what does the
declaration say? If it is lump coal, the bin does not hold the same number of tons as if it is fine coal.
The same kind of coal in each case; the specifications require it.
That does not say what kind it is.

I gave
the figures as to cost.

That does not help. It
depends on how you put the coal in the bin, and how much is in the bin, and the cubic contents of the bin can be ascertained without difficulty, provided it is honestly measured. The computation as to the number of tons the bin holds is not difficult, after you have the cubic contents.
But everything depends upon the kind of coal you put in. If you put in buckwheat you can get in more tons than if you put in run of mine. And if you put in nut coal you certainly can get in more tons than if you put in lump coal. I am merely mentioning that because it shows what a minister of the crown will do, and it gives point and effect to the observations of the hon. member for Parry Sound.
I used the same language the other evening with respect to Mr. Sowards as my learned friend from Parry Sound has used with
[Mr. Rogers. 1
respect to these men. I used the exact language, that they were being attacked without a chance to be heard. Mr. Sowards defence is that he offered to supply coal cheaper than somebody else, and that the taxpayers of Canada would gain thousands of dollars. But we will not have that contract, because the reports received concerning this firm-
It was S600 or so, more expensive than the other.

Now it appears that the
reports have come from the Minister of Labour, who lives in Kingston, where Mr. Sowards lives. That hearsay evidence, if I may so describe it to my hon. friend from Parry Sound, is based upon-

Sworn
evidence.

No; the hearsay evidence of the minister is based upon the information received from Mr. Gibson. And a week ago to-morrow Mr. Gibson, who is a cheese-maker, swears with respect to the contents of the coal bin.
What is wrong with a cheese-maker doing it?
Not a bit.
He swears not only as to the contents of the bin, but as to the bills for coal deliveries.
Yes, certainly, the number of tons supplied.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the cost.

Yes, and the cost. And the same things I have heard with respect to the present supply of coal in other portions of this dominion. I have always said that coal is one of those things in connection with which it is impossible to estimate the number of tons unless you know definitely the size of the coal which goes into the bin.

I do not wish to prolong the discussion, but if the item comes up
again I am prepared to have corroborative testimony with respect to even larger contracts supplied for the Rockwood hospital at Kingston.
It will be observed that it is a provincial institution.
Taken from the public accounts.

It might also be well to remember that Mr. Gibson is an employee of the provincial government, and Mr. Sowards

Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
has been supplying, as the lowest tenderer, coal to the dominion public undertakings for years. What is more, Mr. Norman who was the lowest tenderer the year before in Kingston, received his coal from Mr. Sowards. And Mr. Norman I am informed was advised he could not do so any more. That is the position.
There is the story as I understand it. It is a singular thing that it should be a minister of a federal department who should go to a provincial department for the purpose of determining this question. John Sowards has been supplying coal to the Dominion of Canada since he was a young man. The accounts are there in the auditor general's reports during all those years, and never have I heard such a statement as that now made. Is it not singular that it comes from the provincial authorities, and from an employee of the provincial government, who is a cheese-maker or an instructor.
With respect to the magistrate, and also with respect to the crown attorney, I will say this to the hon. member for Parry Sound, that at least it is laid down in the books that when they have jurisdiction, and an individual is charged with an offence under the criminal code, it is the duty of the law officers and the duty of the magistrate to see that appropriate proceedings are taken, when it is clear that the present proceedings are under a statute that has no availability.

Surely my right hon. friend would not carry that doctrine to the length of saying that where a crown attorney honestly investigates facts and alleged charges, and decides they cannot prevail, he should still scrape up some other charge to lay against a man.
No.
Surely not.

That is not what I said.
What happened in this case was that the magistrate said, "I have no jurisdiction; these cases have all been dealt with under the elections act. It is true this is not under the criminal code, and I will let him go."
He was quite right.

Was he? Well, that is the first time I have heard any reputable counsel say so. The court of criminal appeal in England said just the opposite, rightly or wrongly. With jurisdiction over the time, place, subject matter and the man-here is a man who has impersonated another-the criminal code provides for this; an information has been laid under the code, and yet
the magistrate states that he has no jurisdiction. The crown attorney did not investigate the merits of the case at all. On the contrary, he made it quite clear that he did not propose to do so. My contention is that this is merely part of the general laxity that prevails. I used it for that purpose as an illustration.
I am glad my right hon. friend has made this explanation, because if he will look up his own language he will find that perhaps in the heat of debate it was much stronger.

I think the thing is
perfectly reasonable. Yesterday we were dealing with the question of employment offices. I say they are no use for the purpose of providing employment. Then there was laxity with respect to the conduct, not only of law and order but generally. The whole atmosphere was saturated with the political viewpoint when these matters were being dealt with.
Surely my right hon. friend does not say that they are no use in securing employment.
Yes, they are no use.
Here is the record of the placements. My right hon. friend has not submitted any evidence to justify a general indictment.
I have submitted evidence, and I say more to my hon. friend; I say that an office which is presided over by a drunken blackmailer is no good.
My right hon. friend was applying it to the whole employment service of Canada.

I said that any office
which is presided over by a drunken blackmailer is no good.
No one would contest that for a moment, if true.
Then our case is settled on that phase of it.
My right hon. friend was speaking of the employment service generally and said it was no use in providing employment.

The minister knows perfectly well I am confining the present discussion to Kingston, so he cannot generalize in that way. I asked the minister to investigate. The hon. member for Parry Sound is perfectly right when he says that gossip is not evidence, but it is slightly different when it is circulated generally in the community.
3762	COMMONS
Supply-Labour-Employment Offices
The minister is to investigate this. There are two men in Kingston, Sam and Harry Abra-hamsky, who are furniture dealers. They have stated in the presence of competent and creditable witnesses that they paid S100 to Mr. Stansbury to be placed on the patronage list in order to sell furniture to the government of Canada. Upon investigation it was found that the minister's private secretary had sent a letter to Kingston saying that the executive had not considered the matter and they were not on the list. These men want their money back. I agree with the hon. member for Parry Sound that street talk is not evidence, but it is striking evidence when a letter from the minister's secretary, written in his absence and seen by others, indicates that that is the condition which prevails, namely, that the executive had not considered the matter and they were not on the list. So much for that.
We come now to the question of the utilization of material. Here is the tender of the Frid Construction Company for the repair work at Fort Henry. This is contract No. 36-87, and it contains this phrase:
Cement will be delivered to the owners' railway siding for this work.
In the body of the contract appear these words which I shall quote so that there will be no misunderstanding:
Cement shall be Portland cement supplied by the owner, delivered on the site.
And again:
The department provides free of cost to contractor and f.o.b. owners' private railway siding all Portland cement.
That cement is the property of the crown. If it is fraudulently converted, that is, used for some purpose other than for which it was consigned-
I gave my right hon. friend the-
Just wait a minute, I am speaking. There must be some valid reason. The Frid Construction Company say they made an arrangement with the government, but I ask: When?
With the deputy minister of highways.
When?

Is my right hon. friend
now attacking the reputation of the Frid Construction Company?

I am saying the Frid
Construction Company took cement which, under the terms of their bid, was for Fort Henry, and used it on the Crain building at Queens.
With the consent of the provincial department of highways.

When? Before or after
they did it?
I shall get that information.

They replaced that cement in November, as the minister said. Keep in mind it was in November it was done and the cement had been taken months before. Let me deal now with the question of paint. Where did the white lead go?

Where was it in the first
place ?

The man who lost his job will tell you where it was. One step more. The Minister of National Defence says he has not been able to find the commandant's report, and I ask him to look for it more carefully.
No. I said definitely he had been communicated with and had said there was no report made at any time to Ottawa.
Who said?
The commandant, this afternoon.
With respect to stone?
Yes; that is my information.
Did the quartermaster say so?
I did not consult him.
Consult the quartermaster.
On a point of order, before recess the right hon. gentleman made a definite statement.
He did not.
Yes, he did. He asked if a report had been made by the commandant of the Royal Military College and I said that there was no report.

The Minister of National Defence should have about him at least some measure of appearance. I said I was in the hands of the minister. Those are the exact words I used. Obviously I had no knowledge, but I understood that there was a report from the commandant with respect to this stone and I wanted the minister to produce it.

During the recess the adjutant-general telephoned the

Business of the House-King's Birthday
commandant, and my information, as a result of that conversation, is that there is no such report. I am giving that information to my right hon. friend as it was given to me.
My information is that there is a report. The quartermaster-general may be the man who made it. That is a matter on which the minister can satisfy himself.
I think we had better clear that up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If it is not the quartermaster-general, who would be next?
That is not the question. The question is. Was a report made by any officer of the Royal Military College to the government here with respect to that stone?
That was not the question.
That is the question now. The Minister of Finance says that is a proper question.
My right hon. friend did not say that before six o'clock.
He said he was in the hands of the minister.
If he will look up Hansard he will find that he said, "I believe there is a report by the commandant of the Royal Military College.
But I said I was in the hands of the minister with respect to who made it.
I inquired during the recess and there is no such report.
I want to know if any officer of the Royal Military College made a report on the movement of stone to the Stansbury property by Drinka?
I am informed there was no report made to Ottawa by any officer of the Royal Military College.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall I report items Nos. 109 and 110 which could not be reported yesterday because the committee was forced to adjourn due on account of there being no quorum?
Yes.

I believe a correction should be made. Item No. Ill was the first one taken up and passed yesterday.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Before announcing the business for Monday, if the house will permit me to do so I should like to say just a word as to the adjournment of last evening. Hansard records the fact that there was not a quorum in the house when it met at eight o'clock. I think it is only right that there should be on the records of Hansard the fact that yesterday was the day on which we were celebrating the King's birthday, and that in front of the houses of parliament there was from seven o'clock until nine the ceremony of the trooping of the colours, which brought very large crowds to the front of the buildings. As a matter of fact, the crowds were so arranged as to make it impossible for hon. members to come from the central gates by the direct approach to the parliament buildings as they are accustomed to do in attending meetings of the house. Several hon. members I know of-myself among them- experienced difficulty in getting to the House of Commons because of the crowds that were about at that time. However, the fact is that most hon. members who were not in the house at the time had been or were witnessing the ceremony of the trooping of the colours. It may have been an excess of patriotism on the king's birthday, or some excess of loyalty towards the flag or the sovereign, but that surely was excusable in the circumstances. I believe that if the hon. members already in the house had waited just a moment or two, as the corridors were pretty well filled with members at the time, it would not have taken above a minute or two to have had the house well filled.
The business on Monday will be any bills that may be on the order paper, and will continue in supply with the departments of Labour, of Mines and Resources, and possibly Public Works. I cannot say in which order they will be taken up.

Before the house rises, dealing with the matter mentioned by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), I think it is only fair to point out that those who were here would have been quite ready to have become parties to an extension of time; but as there is no house unless there are twenty present, no motion could be put, nor could the house be adjourned until nine o'clock. It was suggested that it might be adjourned until nine o'clock; but the house cannot be adjourned unless there are twenty people in it, because the constitution itself
Questions

provides in section 48 that it is necessary to have twenty people in order that the house may exercise its powers. Therefore there is no house unless and until there are twenty people in it, and a motion of any kind cannot be made.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am not taking exception to the fact that attention was drawn to the bell, but if the bell had been kept ringing a little longer there would have been enough members present.
We waited five minutes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps if the house had sung God Save the King for five minutes, the chamber would have been filled.

speechtext:
1.	Did the government of Canada recently enter into an agreement with Air. C. J. Sedgwick, of Chelan, Saskatchewan, for the supply of poplar fence posts for a community pasture ?
2.	If so, how many posts were ordered, and what is the agreed price per post, treated and loaded on cars?

maintopic: GOVERNMENT PURCHASE OF FENCE POSTS IN SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
1.	No.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
If the house had sung it for all that time there would not have been anyone left.
It would have been a thin house.

It being eight minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Monday, June 13, 1938
